lead.t: Cryptorchidism is a testis that has not descended into the base of the scrotum.

b: Failure of complete testicular descent from the abdomen into the scrotum. Present in ~1% of 1-year-old males. Both bilateral and unilateral forms are associated with tubular atrophy and sterility.
Microscopic tubular atrophy evident by age 5–6 years; hyalinization by puberty.
Foci of intratubular germ cell neoplasia develop within atrophic tubules — precursors to germ cell tumours.
Carries 3–5 fold increased risk of testicular cancer; history of cryptorchidism found in ~10% of all testicular cancer cases.
Contralateral descended testis also carries increased cancer risk.

snip.t: Risk factors: cryptorchidism (3 to 8 times; the risk persists after orchidopexy), a family history (father or brother), a previous testicular cancer (contralateral), infertility, HIV, hypospadias, carcinoma in situ, in-utero exposure (DES), and Klinefelter's syndrome.
History: was the testis ever palpable in the scrotum? previous inguinal surgery, prematurity, maternal hormones, family history of cryptorchidism, hypospadias, infertility or intersex.

qs.q: A young male patient is found to have an undescended testis (cryptorchidism). Which of the following long-term complications remains a significant risk even after successful surgical correction via orchiopexy?
qs.e: Cryptorchidism is associated with an increased risk of germ cell tumors, and this malignancy risk persists even after surgical correction (orchiopexy), though correction allows for earlier detection. Undescended testes also carry an increased infertility risk.

qs.q: A patient with a history of cryptorchidism is evaluated for long-term complications. Which microscopic change is anticipated in the undescended testis by the time of puberty?
o: Hyperplasia of the Leydig cell population
qs.e: Cryptorchidism leads to progressive microscopic tubular atrophy by age 5–6 years and pronounced hyalinization by puberty. This differs from acute inflammatory states which present with neutrophilic infiltrates instead of hyalinized tubules.

qs.q: A 30-year-old male is investigated for infertility and a history of cryptorchidism corrected during childhood. What is the approximate magnitude of increased testicular cancer risk associated with cryptorchidism?
qs.e: Cryptorchidism confers a 3 to 5 fold increased risk of developing testicular cancer and is present in approximately 10 percent of all testicular cancer cases. A family history involving affected brothers increases risk by 8 to 10 fold.
